I am sixty years old, and I have worked these three *mu* in Quzhou County for forty years. My household has six people, and some of the younger ones have off-farm jobs in town, so I must manage the labor peaks myself. I have a well, and I know the soil here — it is good North China Plain loam, but the groundwater is not infinite, so I do not waste water.

It is the start of the season. For me, that means autumn wheat sowing is approaching. After the maize is harvested and the stalks are chopped, I will **plough** the entire three *mu* to prepare a clean seedbed for wheat. I will sow an **improved** wheat variety around early October. I apply base fertilizer — compound fertilizer and some potash — and I split the nitrogen: half at sowing, half topdressed at jointing in spring. I will irrigate three times: the overwinter water before the deep cold, the jointing water in March, and the heading water in April. I will spray herbicide once in early spring, and if powdery mildew or aphids appear, I will spray once more. I expect about **500 kg per mu** if the winter is kind.

Immediately after wheat harvest in early June, I cannot rest. I will sow **hybrid** maize the same day or the next into the wheat stubble using **no-tillage** direct seeding. I learned long ago that losing even three days at this transition costs yield in September. I put down starter fertilizer with the seed, then topdress with urea at the big-trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice if the summer rains are insufficient — once around tasseling, once at grain filling. I will spray herbicide after emergence and insecticide for corn borer once in July. I expect **550 kg per mu** from the maize.

This is the rhythm I have followed for decades. The key is discipline at the harvest-sowing gap.
